questions.text: You are ramp-checked by an FAA inspector during a fuel stop on a cross-country flight. You present your pilot certificate and a valid Third-Class medical certificate. The inspector says you are still missing one required item under 14 CFR 61.3. What is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Your pilot logbook showing recent flight time

options.label: B
options.text: A government-issued photo identification

options.label: C
options.text: Your aircraft registration certificate

options.label: D
options.text: A printed copy of your most recent flight review endorsement

questions.explanation: Under 14 CFR 61.3(a), a pilot must have in their personal possession or readily accessible in the aircraft: (1) a valid pilot certificate, (2) a current and appropriate medical certificate, and (3) a government-issued photo identification. The photo ID requirement is the most commonly forgotten item on ramp checks. The pilot logbook and flight review endorsement are NOT required to be carried during flight — they must be producible upon request within a reasonable time, but not in the cockpit. The aircraft registration is an aircraft document (14 CFR 91.203), not a pilot document.

questions.text: A 42-year-old private pilot holds a Third-Class medical certificate issued on June 15, 2024. Under 14 CFR 61.23, on what date does this medical certificate expire for private pilot privileges?

options.label: C
options.text: December 31, 2024

questions.explanation: Under 14 CFR 61.23(d), a Third-Class medical certificate for a pilot age 40 or older at the time of examination is valid for 24 calendar months after the month of the exam date. Issued June 15, 2024: 24 calendar months = June 2026, and the calendar month rule extends validity to the END of that month — June 30, 2026. The June 15, 2026 answer is the day-for-day trap. The June 30, 2029 answer reflects 60 months, which applies to pilots UNDER 40.

questions.text: A private pilot accepts full reimbursement from a passenger for a sightseeing flight. Beyond the regulatory violation of 14 CFR 61.113, what compounding safety risk does this create?

options.label: A
options.text: The aircraft must undergo an additional preflight airworthiness inspection

options.label: B
options.text: The passenger becomes legally classified as a required crewmember

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot must file an IFR flight plan with ATC before departure

options.label: D
options.text: The flight may invalidate the aircraft's hull and liability insurance, leaving pilot and passenger financially exposed in an accident

questions.explanation: Most GA aircraft insurance policies contain exclusion clauses for 'for hire' operations or flights inconsistent with the pilot's certificate privileges. Violating 14 CFR 61.113 by accepting full compensation exposes the pilot to FAA certificate action AND can render the insurance void at the moment of greatest need — leaving accident victims and the pilot personally liable for all damages, medical costs, and hull loss.

questions.text: You had not flown in 5 months. Yesterday, you flew solo and completed 3 takeoffs and full-stop landings in calm winds to regain your 90-day passenger currency under 14 CFR 61.57. Today you plan to fly your family in gusty crosswind conditions. What is the PRIMARY safety concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Your medical certificate may have expired during the 5-month gap

options.label: B
options.text: High-time pilots are immune to proficiency decay due to their experience base

options.label: C
options.text: Your 3 landings yesterday were in calm winds, so they do not count toward passenger currency in gusty conditions

options.label: D
options.text: You are legally current but may lack the proficiency to safely handle gusty crosswinds after a 5-month break — 3 calm-wind landings yesterday do not rebuild crosswind skills

questions.explanation: This is the 'current but not proficient' trap documented in FAA-H-8083-2A. The pilot met the legal minimum of 14 CFR 61.57 yesterday — 3 takeoffs and landings. But those were in calm winds. The FAR does not require specific conditions for currency landings — the claim that calm-wind landings fail to count toward currency in gusty conditions is wrong, because the landings DO count legally. The danger is that legal currency is a minimum threshold, not a proficiency guarantee. Three calm-wind landings after a 5-month break do not restore crosswind handling skills. The NTSB has cited this exact proficiency gap in fatal crosswind accidents.

questions.text: You and two friends plan to fly from KPDK to KTYS for a college football game you all want to attend. Total fuel and aircraft rental cost is $300. Your friend offers to pay the full $300. What is the maximum you can legally accept from both passengers combined?

options.label: A
options.text: $0 — private pilots may never accept any payment from passengers

options.label: B
options.text: $200 — your two passengers' pro-rata share of the total

options.label: C
options.text: $150 — passengers may only pay half of total costs

options.label: D
options.text: $300 — passengers may cover all operating costs

questions.explanation: With 3 people on board (you + 2 passengers), each person's pro-rata share is $300 / 3 = $100. You must pay your own $100 share. The maximum you can collect from the two passengers combined is $200. Accepting $300 means you pay nothing — that constitutes full compensation, violating 14 CFR 61.113(c). The 'common purpose' test is satisfied because all three of you are attending the game.

questions.text: Your medical certificate expired last week. You hold a valid pilot certificate and your flight review is current. A friend invites you on a VFR flight and offers to let you fly the entire trip as sole manipulator of the controls while they sit right seat. Can you legally act as pilot in command?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — a valid pilot certificate is all that is required to act as PIC

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — the medical requirement only applies when carrying passengers for hire

options.label: C
options.text: No — you may not act as PIC or as a required pilot flight crewmember without a current medical certificate or BasicMed qualification

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — as long as your friend holds a valid medical, you can fly under their medical authority

questions.explanation: Under 14 CFR 61.23(a), a person must hold a current and appropriate medical certificate (or qualify under BasicMed per 14 CFR Part 68) to exercise the privileges of a pilot certificate. Without a valid medical, you cannot act as PIC or as a required pilot flight crewmember — regardless of whether passengers are aboard or whether the flight is for compensation. A valid pilot certificate alone is not sufficient.

questions.text: You are current (3 landings within 90 days, flight review valid) but you have not flown in 80 days. Weather is VFR with light winds. Your spouse wants to fly to visit family 150 nautical miles away this afternoon. All four actions below are legal. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Cancel the trip entirely — you have not flown in too long, and there is no way to get comfortable again before this afternoon

options.label: B
options.text: Depart this afternoon — 80 days is not that long, and calm conditions are well within your ability as a 300-hour pilot

options.label: C
options.text: Fly a few solo traffic patterns this morning to shake off the rust, then honestly assess whether you feel sharp enough for the cross-country with your spouse aboard

options.label: D
options.text: Depart this afternoon — you are current, weather is good, and the family is expecting you for dinner tonight

questions.sjt_rationale: All four options are legal — the pilot is current. Departing because the family expects you focuses on the destination and external expectations (get-there-itis). Departing because 80 days seems short to a 300-hour pilot dismisses the proficiency gap through overconfidence (macho). Canceling the trip entirely treats the situation as hopeless when a reasonable middle path exists (resignation). Flying solo traffic patterns first is safest because it introduces a self-assessment step: fly solo first, evaluate your own proficiency honestly, then make the go/no-go decision based on how you actually perform.
questions.explanation: FAA-H-8083-2A emphasizes that legal currency is the floor, not the ceiling. Personal minimums and honest self-assessment using PAVE bridge the gap between 'legal to fly' and 'safe to fly.' A pilot who has not flown in 80 days may be current, but their proficiency has likely degraded. The safest action is to test yourself before committing passengers to the flight. Reference: NTSB Safety Alert SA-019 ('Reduced Proficiency in General Aviation Pilots'); FAA-H-8083-2A Chapter 2 (Aeronautical Decision Making); NTSB CAROL search: 'proficiency' + 'currency' + 'fatal' documents repeated pattern of current-but-not-proficient pilots in LOC-I accidents.

questions.text: You arrive at the airport with two passengers for a long-planned cross-country trip. While preflighting, you realize you left your wallet — containing your government-issued photo ID — at home, a 45-minute drive away. Under 14 CFR 61.3, you cannot legally act as PIC without it. Your passengers have a tight schedule and marginal weather is forecast to move in later this afternoon. All four actions below are legal. Which is the SAFEST aeronautical decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Drive home to get the ID, accept the delay, and re-evaluate the weather forecast and flight plan with the adjusted departure time before deciding to go

options.label: B
options.text: Drive home to get it, assuring your passengers you can still beat the approaching weather because you know the route well and fly fast

options.label: C
options.text: Cancel the entire trip immediately — the schedule is ruined and it is not worth the hassle of driving home and back

options.label: D
options.text: Drive home to get it, then skip your planned en-route fuel stop to make up the lost 90 minutes

questions.sjt_rationale: All four options acknowledge the legal requirement (you must go get the ID). The differentiation is in what happens AFTER. Skipping the planned en-route fuel stop to make up time introduces physical risk by reducing fuel reserves (get-there-itis). Promising passengers the weather is beatable is a macho overconfidence trap when the weather is already described as marginal. Canceling the trip entirely when a reasonable middle path exists is resignation. The safest path accepts the delay without compounding new risks: drive home, get the ID, then re-evaluate whether the trip is still safe given the new timeline and evolving weather.
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 61.3(a) requires a government-issued photo ID to act as PIC. The forgotten ID creates a 90-minute delay that pressures the pilot into poor risk management decisions. FAA-H-8083-2A identifies this exact pattern: an initial setback (the delay) triggers hazardous attitudes that compound risk. The safest response is to solve the original problem (get the ID) WITHOUT introducing new risks (skipping fuel, racing weather, or abandoning the trip unnecessarily). Reference: FAA-H-8083-2A Chapter 2 (Hazardous Attitudes: Get-There-Itis, Macho, Resignation); FAA Order 2150.3C (enforcement pattern for 61.3 violations confirms this is an active ramp-check enforcement priority, not a theoretical risk).
